result: The Danish swIAV surveillance program received 3800 submissions from 2011-2018, with swIAV-positive submissions increasing from 36% in 2011 to 56% in 2018. Submissions peaked during autumn/winter months (October-March), but no consistent seasonal variation in swIAV positivity was observed, with monthly averages ranging from 42.6-51.8%.
evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C36-C43 provide consistent data on submission numbers, temporal patterns, and positivity rates. The data are directly derived from surveillance records and shown in Figure 1 and supplements. Statistical analysis (C42, C49) confirms lack of significant seasonal variation in positivity despite seasonal submission patterns.

result: H1pdm09-positive submissions showed temporal variation, starting at 21% in 2011, decreasing to 14-16% in 2012-2013, then increasing in 2014 and stabilizing at 20-26% from 2014-2018. No significant seasonal variation in H1pdm09 prevalence was detected (p>0.05).
evaluation: Claims C44-C49 and C143 present consistent temporal data on H1pdm09 prevalence with appropriate statistical testing. The lack of seasonality is explicitly tested (C49) and corroborated by comparison with French data (C143). Data are shown in Figure 1a and supplement 2.

result: Lineage determination improved from 33-48% (2011-2014) to 61-77% (2015-2018) of swIAV-positive submissions due to implementation of multiplex RT-PCR/Fluidigm. H1N2dk was the most prevalent lineage, increasing from 42% (2012) to 69% (2018), while H1avN1av decreased from 30-37% (2011-2012) to 5% (2018). H1N1pdm09 remained relatively stable at ~16% (exception: 25.6% in 2015).
evaluation: Claims C50-C56 describe lineage distribution changes supported by surveillance data in Figure 1b. The methodological improvement (C50-C51) explains increased lineage determination success. Temporal trends are consistent and data-driven, though the cause of 2015 H1N1pdm09 spike (C56) is not explained.

result: Six novel reassortant strains were identified during 2011-2018 surveillance: H1pdmN2dk (first detected 2011, stable at ~4% with peaks in 2016/2018), H1pdmN2hu95 (2011-2017, 1-3.2%, absent in 2016/2018), H1avN1pdm and H1pdmN1av (both 2018), H3hu05N2dk (2013-2018, except 2017), and H1avN2hu95 (2011-2018, except 2016).
evaluation: Claims C57-C74 document novel reassortants with specific detection dates, prevalence data, and genomic compositions. Data are consistent across claims and supported by Figure 1b. The inverse relationship between H1pdmN2dk and H1pdmN2hu95 detection (C60, C64) is interesting but unexplained.

result: Full-genome sequencing was performed on 129 swIAV-positive samples (128 uploaded to GenBank: MT666225-MT667233), yielding 78 H1av, 48 H1pdm09, 3 H3hu05 HA sequences, and 32 N1pdm, 14 N1av, 75 N2dk, 8 N2hu95 NA sequences. Analysis identified 17 different genotypes.
evaluation: Claims C4, C75-C76, C104, C127 provide consistent counts of sequenced samples. Minor discrepancy: C4 states 129 samples, C75 states 128 uploaded, explained by inclusion of one previously published sequence (C75 context). Sequence counts and genotype numbers are data-derived and internally consistent.

result: H1av sequences showed high nucleotide diversity (π=0.099, SE=0.0005) and dispersed into multiple clusters without typical influenza ladder-like structure. Low correlation existed between sampling time and genetic divergence. Danish sequences represented 9 of 10 European H1av clusters (Henritzi et al. 2020), with one unique Danish cluster. All belonged to clade 1.C.2 by IRD classification. One cluster was dominated by strains with H1N1pdm09 internal genes.
evaluation: Claims C77-C87 present phylogenetic analysis results supported by Figure 2 and Table 1. Diversity metrics (C77-C78) are quantitative. Phylogenetic patterns (C79-C84) are visually supported. IRD classification (C85-C86) is based on standard tool. The suggestion to expand IRD classification (C86) is reasonable inference from observed clustering patterns.

result: CODEML analysis provided strong evidence for positive selection in H1av sequences, with four codons under positive selection (high dN/dS ratios under M2a model), all located in the globular head of HA protein in previously defined antigenic sites.
evaluation: Claims C88-C89 report CODEML results shown in Table 1. The analysis appropriately compares M1a vs M2a models. Identification of positively selected sites in antigenic regions is biologically meaningful and supported by the data. Methods are standard for detecting selection.

result: H1pdm09 sequences showed lower diversity than H1av (π=0.043, SE=0.0005). Phylogenetic analysis revealed 30 Danish sequences (collected 2015-2018) formed a swine-only 'Sw-L cluster', while 18 sequences (2013-2017) branched basally with human/swine sequences. Sequences evolved temporally with substitution rate 4.9×10⁻³ per site/year; Sw-L cluster common ancestor dated ~2014.
evaluation: Claims C90-C96 present consistent phylogenetic and molecular clock analysis supported by Figure 3, Table 1, and supplements. Diversity calculation (C90), cluster identification (C91-C92), temporal patterns (C93-C94), and evolutionary rate estimation (C95-C96) are all data-driven. BEAST and TempEst analyses are appropriate methods.

result: Amino acid comparison identified 20 positions distinguishing Sw-L cluster from other H1pdm09 sequences, with 6 positions 100% unique to Sw-L cluster. Five of six unique positions were in antigenic sites (Ca, Sb) or receptor binding site (RBS). No unique swine/human residues were found in broader comparison, but position 273 showed significantly more A in swine (91%) vs human (27%) sequences (p<0.05).
evaluation: Claims C97-C101 report amino acid analysis results shown in Table 2. The identification of cluster-defining residues (C97-C98) and their functional locations (C99) are data-supported. Statistical comparison at position 273 (C101) is appropriately tested. The lack of universal swine/human markers (C100) is a negative result but clearly stated.

result: Three H3 sequences showed low nucleotide diversity (π=0.027, SE=0.002), with closest human match being A/Denmark/129/2005(H3N2) (accession EU103786) for all three sequences.
evaluation: Claims C102-C103 report basic sequence analysis. Diversity calculation (C102) is straightforward. BLAST identification of closest match (C103) is standard methodology. Limited sample size (n=3) appropriately noted, with authors stating no further analysis performed.

result: N1pdm09 sequences (n=32) showed nucleotide diversity π=0.029 (SE=0.0005). Majority of 2015-2018 sequences clustered together, while 2013-2014 sequences were outside cluster. TempEst showed high correlation with time; BEAST analysis revealed substitution rate 3.9×10⁻³ per site/year. No evidence of positive selection was found.
evaluation: Claims C105-C109 present NA gene analysis supported by Figure 3-supplement 2 and Table 3. Diversity metrics (C105), phylogenetic patterns (C106), temporal evolution (C107-C108), and selection analysis (C109) are consistently reported. Methods parallel those for HA analysis.

result: N1av sequences (n=14) showed high nucleotide diversity (π=0.097, SE=0.003) similar to H1av. No clear clustering was observed. TempEst showed relatively low correlation between genetic divergence and time. BEAST revealed substitution rate 5.9×10⁻³ per site/year. No positive selection was detected.
evaluation: Claims C110-C114 report N1av analysis supported by Figure 3-supplement 3 and Table 3. High diversity (C110) parallels H1av pattern. Lack of clear clustering (C111) and low temporal correlation (C112) are consistent with H1av surface gene patterns. Substitution rate (C113) and selection analysis (C114) are appropriately reported.

result: N2dk sequences (n=75) showed nucleotide diversity π=0.08 (SE=0.0005) with six main clusters. Clusters showed no temporal clustering. One major cluster contained only HxN2dk strains with full/partial H1N1pdm09 internal genes, overlapping 28/30 samples with H1av cluster 3. TempEst/BEAST showed low temporal correlation and substitution rate 4.4×10⁻³ per site/year. No positive selection detected.
evaluation: Claims C115-C121 present N2dk analysis supported by Figure 3-supplement 4 and Table 3. The correlation between N2dk and H1av clustering by internal gene origin (C118-C119) is an important finding showing co-evolution of surface and internal genes. All metrics are data-supported.

result: N2hu95 sequences (n=8) showed diversity π=0.085 (SE=0.006). Despite limited samples, Bayesian analysis revealed two clusters: one with full avian internal genes, one with full/partial H1N1pdm09 internal genes. TempEst showed low temporal correlation. Substitution rate not reported due to overestimation from low sample size. No positive selection detected.
evaluation: Claims C122-C125 report N2hu95 analysis supported by Figure 3-supplement 5 and Table 3. Authors appropriately acknowledge limitations of small sample size (C124) and exclude unreliable substitution rate. Clustering by internal gene origin (C123) parallels N2dk pattern. Analysis is appropriately cautious given limited data.

result: Examination of all 129 NA sequences across different lineages found no amino acid changes associated with NA inhibitor resistance or increased virulence.
evaluation: Claim C126 reports negative finding from systematic screening of known resistance/virulence markers. This is an important surveillance result indicating no immediate antiviral resistance concerns. The analysis is straightforward comparison against known markers.

result: Genotype analysis showed H1N2dk, H1avN1av, and H1avN2hu95 had highest genotypic diversity, while strains with H1N1pdm09 surface genes typically had complete H1N1pdm09 internal genes. All internal genes (M, NP, NS, PA, PB1, PB2) formed two main clusters (H1avN1av vs H1N1pdm09 origin). Since 2013, increasing numbers of H1N2dk acquired H1N1pdm09 internal genes; H1avN2hu95 showed similar trend. H1avN1av maintained avian-like internal genes (3 exceptions). All H1N1pdm09 surface gene reassortants had complete H1N1pdm09 internal genes (1 exception). All three H3hu05N2dk had complete H1N1pdm09 internal genes.
evaluation: Claims C128-C135 describe genotype patterns supported by Table 4 and source data 1-7. The temporal trend of H1N2dk acquiring H1N1pdm09 internal genes (C131) is a major finding shown in source data 7. Patterns are consistent across claims. Exceptions are appropriately noted (C133-C134).

result: Statistical analysis revealed no significant seasonal differences in swIAV prevalence, contradicting traditional view of autumn/winter disease. This supports recent studies on enzootic persistence, likely due to modern herd management. Similar patterns observed in other European countries. Possible explanations for increased autumn/winter submissions include more severe clinical signs, co-circulation of other respiratory pathogens, or veterinary perception biases. No seasonality in H1pdm09 prevalence was documented.
evaluation: Claims C136-C144 present seasonality analysis with appropriate statistical testing (C136, C49) and comparison to literature (C137, C139, C140, C143). The lack of seasonality is well-supported by data in Figure 1-supplements 1-2. Alternative explanations for submission patterns (C140-C142) are speculative but reasonable. The interpretation about enzootic persistence (C137-C138) is supported by citations.

result: H1N1pdm09 rapidly spread after 2010 introduction and nearly replaced H1avN1av. H3N2 almost disappeared from Denmark. H1N2dk increased in prevalence and gradually acquired H1N1pdm09 internal genes, suggesting this gene constellation is beneficial. General increase in Danish swIAV carrying H1N1pdm09 internal genes indicates this is advantageous.
evaluation: Claims C145-C150 describe major lineage shifts supported by Figure 1b and genomic data. The replacement of H1avN1av by H1N1pdm09 (C145) and disappearance of H3N2 (C146) are clearly shown. The acquisition of H1N1pdm09 internal genes by H1N2dk (C147, C131) is well-documented. The inference of benefit/advantage (C148, C150) is reasonable from prevalence data but remains correlative.

result: Potential explanations for H1N1pdm09 internal gene advantage include: better polymerase replication efficiency (Ma et al. 2015), enhanced transmissibility of certain gene combinations (Chou 2011), and possible influence on surface gene evolution. Replacement of avian internal genes with H1N1pdm09 genes could enhance zoonotic potential, as seen with American H3N2v and British H1N2hu lineages that caused human infections.
evaluation: Claims C151-C155 propose mechanisms for observed patterns but are largely speculative. Citations support individual mechanisms (C151-C152, C155) but don't directly test them in this system. The influence on surface gene evolution (C153) is inferred from clustering patterns but not experimentally validated. These are reasonable hypotheses requiring further investigation.

result: H3hu05N2dk triple-reassortant (enzootic swIAV + H1N1pdm09 + human seasonal IAV genes) was only sporadically detected despite potential for devastating consequences due to lack of population immunity. This, combined with H1N2dk success despite high HA immunity since 1990s, suggests factors beyond preexisting HA immunity drive swIAV spread and evolution, potentially including internal gene cassette fitness.
evaluation: Claims C156-C162 present important observations about H3hu05N2dk rarity (C157) and H1N2dk success (C160) that challenge assumptions about immunity-driven evolution. However, the inference that other factors are more important (C159, C162) is speculative. The suggestion to reconsider HA immunity as sole driver (C162) is reasonable but not definitively proven. Alternative explanations (founder effects, transmission bottlenecks) not fully explored.

result: H1avN2hu95 and H1pdmN2hu95 reassortants are concerning from zoonotic perspective because 7-8 gene segments originate from human IAVs, suggesting adaptation for human replication/transmission. H1avN2hu95 particularly concerning as spillover would introduce novel HA with limited cross-immunity.
evaluation: Claims C163-C165 raise valid zoonotic concerns based on genomic composition. The inference of human adaptation (C164) from gene origin is logical but not experimentally validated. The concern about limited cross-immunity to H1av (C165) is supported by citations (Sun et al. 2020, Henritzi et al. 2020) but actual zoonotic risk remains unquantified. These are important surveillance findings but risk assessment is qualitative.

result: H1av underwent extensive genetic/antigenic drift with evolution in multiple directions rather than single direction, creating numerous clusters/variants. This confirms recent European studies (Henritzi et al. 2020). Unlike single-herd pectinate pattern observed previously (Ryt-Hansen et al. 2020), national/global scale shows disrupted pattern. This difference likely reflects that human population acts as single epidemiological unit due to global interactions, while swine herds represent multiple closed epidemiological units with individual pectinate patterns.
evaluation: Claims C166-C175 present important evolutionary insights. High H1av diversity (C166-C167) is well-documented (Figure 2, Table 1). Comparison with previous single-herd study (C169-C171) is valid. The hypothesis about scale-dependent patterns (C172-C175) is speculative but logically coherent and explains apparent contradiction. The epidemiological unit concept (C174-C175) is reasonable but not directly tested.

result: Despite lack of pectinate evolution pattern, H1av protein showed clear positive selection at codons in antigenic sites, known to alter neutralizing antibody binding. This confirms herd immunity drives antigenic drift in HA globular head as in human seasonal IAV. Similar residues under selection across herds suggests particular importance for swIAV evolution. H1av substitution rate (4.6×10⁻³ per site/year) was similar to previous studies but lower than single-herd estimate, emphasizing need to differentiate single-herd vs surveillance-based evolutionary results.
evaluation: Claims C176-C182 integrate selection analysis with evolutionary rate estimation. Positive selection in antigenic sites (C176, C89) is well-supported by CODEML analysis (Table 1). Connection to antibody binding (C177) and antigenic drift (C178) is supported by citations. Observation of similar residues under selection (C179) is interesting but limited by sample size. Substitution rate comparisons (C180-C182) appropriately cite previous work and note scale-dependent differences.

result: H1pdm09 analysis revealed swine-only Sw-L cluster, with remaining sequences scattered among human seasonal sequences. Similar pattern described in two European studies (Chastagner et al. 2018, Henritzi et al. 2020), suggesting swine-adapted vs reverse-zoonotic groups. Majority of amino acid differences between Sw-L and other sequences located in antigenic sites/RBS, indicating probable host adaptation. Danish Sw-L cluster separated from French swine-derived cluster, indicating different evolutionary trajectories in non-connected populations.
evaluation: Claims C183-C189 describe important H1pdm09 divergence. Sw-L cluster identification (C183, C91) is well-supported by Figure 3. Comparison with European studies (C184) validates pattern. Interpretation as swine-adapted vs reverse-zoonotic (C185) is reasonable speculation. Amino acid analysis (C186-C187) supports adaptation hypothesis. Separation from French cluster (C188-C189) is important finding showing independent evolution, though sample sizes for comparison not specified.

result: French antigenic cartography showed high cross-protection between swine-adapted and human seasonal-like H1N1pdm09 (2014-2016), but Danish Sw-L cluster differs from French cluster, warranting repeat analysis. Data indicate human seasonal H1N1pdm09 can still infect swine after 10+ years human adaptation, but unclear if Sw-L viruses retained human infectivity. Divergent evolution in pigs vs humans is concerning if Sw-L viruses can infect humans.
evaluation: Claims C190-C194 discuss zoonotic implications. French cross-protection data (C190) is cited but Danish-French differences (C191) suggest caution in extrapolation. Inference about continued swine susceptibility to human viruses (C192) is reasonable from phylogenetic data but not experimentally tested. Uncertainty about Sw-L human infectivity (C193) is appropriately stated. Zoonotic concern (C194) is valid but risk level unquantified. Ferret studies mentioned as ongoing but not reported.

result: H1pdm09 HA proteins appear better adapted for α2.6-linked sialic acid receptor binding than H1av, possibly reflecting H1pdm09's 100+ year mammalian circulation (descended from Spanish flu) vs H1av's 1980s mammalian detection. This may explain few H1av zoonotic cases. More H1pdm09 sequences outside Sw-L cluster had D at position 225, supporting their similarity to human seasonal viruses and suggesting G225D transition more important in humans than swine.
evaluation: Claims C195-C200 propose receptor binding differences and evolutionary explanations. Receptor binding inference (C195) is based on residue analysis but not functional assays. Historical context (C196-C197) is citation-supported. Connection to zoonotic cases (C198) is correlative. Position 225 analysis (C199-C200) is data-supported but functional significance of G225D in swine vs humans not experimentally validated. These are reasonable hypotheses requiring functional validation.

result: Eight amino acid residues previously defined to differ between avian IAVs and H1N1pdm09 in NP, PB1, PB2, PA were consistent with Danish sequence clusters, suggesting specificity for H1pdmNx swIAV. MxA resistance residues (48Q, 98K, 99K) in H1avN1av NP were present in 81% of Danish H1avN1av NP proteins. MxA resistance is believed important for zoonotic/pandemic potential, indicating potential increased zoonotic transmission risk in Danish herds with these mutations.
evaluation: Claims C201-C206 report internal gene markers. Consistency with previously defined residues (C201-C202) validates prior findings. MxA resistance residue prevalence (C203-C204) is clearly quantified. Connection to zoonotic potential (C205) is citation-supported. Inference of increased risk (C206) is reasonable but actual risk level unquantified. The analysis appropriately identifies concerning markers for surveillance.

result: Amino acid differences between Sw-L cluster and outside sequences in internal genes include: T76A in PB2 (linked to elevated interferon response), M283I in PB2 (linked to decreased H5 virulence), N456S in PB2 (linked to H3N2 human adaptation), M317I in PB1 (identified in temperature-sensitive strain), and C241Y in PA (linked to H5N1 mammalian adaptation). Several differences previously described to influence virulence, replication efficiency, or host-response/adaptation, emphasizing potential importance in H1pdm09Nx swine adaptation.
evaluation: Claims C207-C213 catalog internal gene differences with literature context. Individual mutations are appropriately cited (C207-C211) but their functions were determined in different viral contexts (H5, H3N2, H2N2). The inference that these changes are important for swine adaptation (C213) is reasonable but not experimentally validated in this system. These are candidates for functional studies but their actual roles in Danish swIAV remain speculative.

result: The surveillance program was essential for identifying novel reassortants/genotypes, supporting vaccine selection and understanding transmission dynamics. Novel reassortants not covered by current vaccines were identified, encouraging vaccine updates based on both novel reassortants and documented antigenic drift (which affects cross-protection). European H1av antigenic mapping revealed huge antigenic distances emphasizing lack of cross-protection within lineage. Increasing submissions in later years indicates program usefulness. The program's ability to identify zoonotic-risk strains is vital as early warning system for future pandemics.
evaluation: Claims C214-C225 discuss surveillance program value. Identification of novel reassortants (C214, C216, C74) is well-documented. Practical applications (C215) are reasonable. Connection to vaccine updates (C216-C217) is logical. Antigenic drift impact (C218) and lack of cross-protection (C219-C220) are citation-supported. Increased submissions (C221-C222) shown in data. Early warning function (C224-C225) is appropriate characterization of surveillance role. These claims appropriately contextualize the study's public health significance.
